title: In Conversation with Jean Lambert, England and Wales
content:
Jean Lambert is a long-standing member of the Green Party of England and Wales, where she has held a number of posts of responsibility. She served as London’s Green Party MEP for four terms (1999-2019) and was a member of the Employment and Social Affairs Committee and the Civil Liberties Committee. Jean chaired the EP’s Delegation to the Countries of South Asia for ten years and took part in a number of Election Observation missions. Prior to her election to the EP, Jean worked as a secondary school teacher in East London. Jean is now a Trustee of the European Network on Statelessness (ENS) and a Board member of a Brussels-based organisation promoting citizens’ rights. She also recently served on the Committee of the European Green Party. She is an avid reader of crime fiction and loves dancing. 

In this interview, Jean Lambert reflects on five decades of Green politics, from its early roots to its influence on the European agenda. She explores the lessons of European cooperation, the challenges of delivering a socially just green transition, and why the movement must keep climate at its core while rediscovering its original imagination and ambition.

title: In Conversation with Natalie Bennett, United Kingdom
content:
Natalie Bennett, Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle, is UK Green politician and former journalist. She led the Green Party of England and Wales from 2012 to 2016 and has been a member of the UK House of Lords since 2019. Before entering politics, she was editor of the Guardian Weekly from 2007 to 2012. She also lived in Thailand for five years, where she volunteered with the National Commission on Women’s Affairs. 

In this interview, Natalie Bennet reflects on her journey from journalism to Green politics, the lessons behind the party’s electoral breakthroughs, and the role of European cooperation. She explores how Greens can gain political power without losing their movement roots, and why the future of Green politics depends on connecting ecological limits with public health, economic justice, and social wellbeing. 

Can you please introduce yourself?

title: In Conversation with Benedeck Jávor, Hungary
content:
Benedek Jávor is a Hungarian Green activist and politician. Originally a biologist, he was an environmental campaigner before entering politics, founding and leading a major green NGO in Hungary. In 2009, he co-founded the first Hungarian Green Party, Politics Can Be Different (LMP), which entered the country’s parliament the following year. He served a four-year mandate as a member of parliament. In 2014, he was elected to the European Parliament, on behalf of a newly created Green Party – Dialogue for Hungary (PM). He currently heads the representation office of the city of Budapest to the EU.

In this interview Benedek Jávor traces the development of Hungary’s Green politics over the past decades, from its emergence out of grassroots environmental struggles, to the ideological divisions that lead to a fundamental schism, and the destructive impact of the Orbán years on a promising political movement that was just beginning to bear fruit.

Can you tell us about the origins of the ecological movement in Hungary, particularly around the end of the communist era?

title: The Greens Hit 50
content:
The 2020s are a pivotal decade, both for the Greens and the world at large. The Greens really began to feel their feet in the 1990s and early 2000s, back when the “end of history” promise of progress was the spirit of the times. What succeeded it has been at least a decade and a half of disorder. Liberal democracy’s struggle to grapple with populism and right-wing authoritarianism, profound technological change, and growing environmental crisis to which the uncertain energy transition is only a partial answer are central elements of this new disorder. 

This same context is also the backdrop for green politics in Europe gaining more political power than ever before. Energised by the global climate awakening, Green parties entered government in 7 EU countries between 2018 and 2021. Their surge pushed the European Commission to put forward its European Green Deal, an ambitious regulatory agenda centred on reaching “net zero” carbon emissions by 2050.

title: The Future of European Green Politics
content: After five decades and unprecedented success – reaching government in 9 of 27 EU member states – European Greens face not just an electoral reversal but an identity crisis. Their surge catalysed the European Green Deal; yet both that agenda and broader progressive commitments have since been dismantled. The question is no longer whether Greens can win elections, but whether they know who they are and what they stand for in a world that has fundamentally changed.

title: In Conversation with Rui Tavares, Portugal
content:
Rui Tavares is a Portuguese writer, historian, and member of the parliament for the left-green-libertarian party LIVRE. He is the author of the documentary film Ulysses: Breaking the Spell of the Crisis to Save Europe. He was formerly an MEP for Greens/EFA.

In this interview Rui Tavares talks about the green movement’s place in the turbulent history of democracy in Portugal and brings back memories of these nuances times.

You can watch the interview here or on our YouTube channel. 

Would you like to introduce yourself and tell us how your personal story leads to LIVRE?

I was born in Portugal in 1972, still under the dictatorship. Our democratic revolution was in April 1974, when I was less than two years old. This context is crucial for our conversation because it reveals that Portuguese democracy and green parties in Europe are both children of the early 1970s, today around 50 years old.

title: Greenhouse Alumni Training – October ’26: Green European Solidarity
content:
This edition of The Greenhouse Training brought together 20 alumni from across Europe for a five-day political ecology training focused on advanced political reflection, strategic debate, peer exchange and strengthening connections across borders and Greenhouse cohorts. The participants explore pressing challenges facing Green politics, exchanged experiences from their own political contexts, and exchanged with some of the leading political voices and organisers in the European Green movement.

From 7-11 October 2026, the Greenhouse Alumni Training brought together 20 participants from 15 European countries to engage in an intensive five-day political ecology training in the Lithuanian countryside. A central theme throughout the training was the foundations and future of the European Green project and how Green movements can reclaim proactive and hopeful stances in the context of increasingly complex, polarised, and crisis-ridden political landscapes.

title: Call for Tenders: Policy Consultant on the Green Transition (CLOSED)
content:
About the Green European Foundation 

The Green European Foundation (GEF) is a European-level political foundation funded by the European Parliament. GEF is affiliated to, but independent from, the European Green Party and Green movement in Europe.  

Our mission is to encourage European citizens to participate in European political discussions and in particular when it comes to envisioning what a Green Europe would look like. As a forum for cooperation at the European level, we work with our national member foundations and thereby aim to stimulate and strengthen the European public debate and the curation of lessons and ideas for a greener Europe.

title: European Green Academy 2026: Democracy, Tech and Civil Society at a Turning Point
content:
The European Green Academy brings together Green and progressive actors, civil society representatives, activists, thinkers, and engaged citizens from across Europe and beyond to exchange ideas, strengthen connections, and reflect collectively on the political challenges shaping our societies. The Academy aims to foster learning, transnational debate, and networking across the wider Green and progressive ecosystem.

This April, the European Green Academy reopened its doors in an exceptionally sunny Brussels for its fourth edition. This year’s edition welcomed over 180 participants, organisations and platforms from more than 35 countries, alongside more than 40 speakers, moderators and trainers, with a strong emphasis on diversity and intergenerational dialogue. Over 1.5 days, participants and speakers came together not only to debate the challenges facing Europe today, but also to collectively reflect on the kind of future Greens and progressives want to build.

title: Greenhouse Training – March ’26: Technology and Democracy
content:
The Greenhouse Training is an intensive residential training for activists, thinkers, organisers, and anyone committed to shaping a vibrant, sustainable, and democratic Europe. Rooted in political ecology education, the training combines participatory methods, community-building, and expert-led workshops and debates. During the training, participants deepen their understanding of the roots and trajectories of the Green movement, explore pressing societal challenges through a European lens, strengthen core competences in areas like rhetoric and debating, and become part of the Greenhouse Community – giving them access to further opportunities for training, networking, and mentorship. 

After a successful pilot edition in Latvia, the second edition of The Greenhouse: Training for Activists took place from 03 to 08 March 2026 in Reggello, Italy. The training gathered 28 participants from 19 countries between the ages of 18 and 32 – all leading change in their local communities. Creating space for exchange, connection, and debate, they were joined by a team of experienced trainers and educators, as well as leading voices from the European Green movement.

title: Connect the Dots
content:
Room: Salle de Guichets 

You’re in the same room as changemakers from across Europe and beyond. Use this half-hour well. Connect the Dots is a structured speed networking session designed to spark real conversations, not small talk. In a few quick rounds, you’ll swap stories, find unexpected common ground, and leave with at least one new connection worth keeping. Come with curiosity. No agenda required. Coffee provided.

Facilitator: Eliza Popper, facilitator, trainer and consultant.

Eliza Popper is an experienced facilitator, trainer, and consultant based in Brussels, who has worked at capacity-building events in over 40 countries. She has extensive experience in the youth and education sector, with a focus on organisational development, youth policy, and youth work. Eliza used to be Ad-Interim Deputy Director of the Green European Foundation, and is the co-founder of the Good Enough Company.

title: Where Do We Go From Here? Shaping AI, Shaping Ourselves
content:
Room: Salle de Guichets

As the programme comes to a close, this session invites participants to step back and reflect on a deeper question: what does AI reveal about us, and what kind of societies do we want to build in response? Drawing on the ideas of The AI Mirror, Shannon Vallor will explore how AI not only shapes our world but also reflects our values, assumptions, and inequalities back to us. Moving from reflection to action, the conversation will consider how these technologies are reshaping human agency, democratic participation, and political responsibility- and where space still exists to resist, rethink, and redirect their trajectory. The session will be open and interactive, leaving room for collective reflection and audience exchange.

Prof. Shannon Vallor, Co-Director, Centre for Technomoral Futures, author The AI Mirror: How to Reclaim Our Humanity in an Age of Machine Thinking

Meyrem Almaci, Co-President, Green European Foundation

Meyrem Almaci, 1976, Belgian with Turkish roots, mother of two; lifelong fan of fantasy, anime, books and good music. Party Leader of Groen (‘14-‘22) , member of Parliament since 2007.  Believes in saving the planet and being a good ancestor for the future generations, whilst also having fun and enjoying life as much as possible. So: Don’t curse the darkness, light a candle.

Vula Tsetsi, Co-chair, European Green Party

Vula Tsetsi has been Co-Chair of the European Green Party since December 2024. Originally from Athens, Greece, she is a trained urban and regional planner and a longstanding figure in the European Green movement. Prior to her current role, Tsetsi served as Secretary General of the Greens/European Free Alliance group in the European Parliament for twenty years, being re-elected to the position five times. As Co-Chair, she has championed a united Green front against the rise of the far right across Europe, while advocating for democracy, LGBTQ+ rights, and a fair green transition for all.

title: Parallel Session
content:
Room: Magritte (+ Delvaux) 

We often ask how progressive movements can respond to democratic erosion – but what is actually working on the ground? This session brings together activists, Greens, and civil society actors to move beyond analysis and into practice. Through direct exchange with frontline practitioners, participants will explore concrete strategies and tactics that are building resilience and momentum across Europe – from shaping narratives and countering the far right, to mobilising people into action, and using institutional levers to defend democracy and civic space.

The session builds toward a shared “tactics map” of real-world approaches – and a critical question to carry forward: how can we scale, adapt, and strengthen these strategies across different contexts?

This is part two of a two-session journey (following Understanding Democratic Erosion from the Ground Up), but can also be attended as a standalone session.

This session is organised in collaboration with the Federation of Young European Greens (FYEG) and GEF Greenhouse alumni & FYEG.

Agata Meysner, Treasurer Green European Foundation; Co-Founder, Generation Climate Europe

title: Parallel Session
content:
Room: Brel 

The notion that Europeans are moving to the right has become common sense. It is repeated in public discourse and media debates, and reflected in parliaments and governments across the continent. Yet there’s evidence that the opposite is true: the values and preferences of European citizens, particularly younger generations and women, are turning more progressive. This potential, however, remains largely untapped as rising numbers of citizens grow distrustful of representation and disengage from parties and elections. As a result, institutional politics is increasingly reflecting and catering to loud, older, and male-dominated conservative minorities. 

What is the role of civil society and Green actors in breaking the vicious circle of abstention and reactionary politics? And how can new forms of engagement among younger generations translate into meaningful political action and representation? 

This session is organised in collaboration with the Green European Journal.  

Imogen Learmonth, Programme Manager, Datapraxis

title: Parallel Session
content:
Room: Zinneke 

The idea of accelerating, disruptive artificial intelligence is ubiquitous. But that this narrative is spun by the very industry it nourishes doesn’t make it untrue. With the increasing adoption of AI and the roll-out of the huge infrastructures needed to sustain it, this technology is reshaping both how we live with profound implications for rights, justice and participation. In this session, participants will explore key questions with experts who will shine a light on different facets of AI, their implications for our democratic societies, and what we can do about it.

Namita Kambli, Project Lead, Centre for Future Generations 

Namita applies a social and environmental lens to the governance of emerging technologies. Her goal is to ensure both people and the planet have a fair shot in decision-making – now and in the future.

Kristina Wilfore, Director of Innovation and Global Projects at Reset Tech
